content: Between May 2018 and February 2019, 555 HIV-positive female index clients were identified, who provided information on 694 male sexual contacts. Of these, 361 male contacts were traced and offered HIV testing. Among those tested, 188 were confirmed as HIV-positive, representing a positivity rate of 52%. Of these, 114 (61%) were already known to be HIV-positive, while 74 (39%) were newly identified as HIV-positive. The newly identified cases accounted for 21% of all male sexual contacts traced and tested, which is a significantly higher yield compared to routine testing methods in the same settings. All individuals diagnosed with HIV were promptly linked to care and treatment services. This approach, known as assisted partner notification services, has proven to be an effective strategy for identifying HIV-positive individuals and ensuring their enrollment in care and treatment programs. It highlights the need for further capacity-building among service providers to enhance counseling, contact elicitation, and tracing efforts. In Vietnam, online platforms have become essential tools for reaching key populations, particularly men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women, who frequently use social media to find sexual partners and access HIV-related information. Online outreach efforts utilize interconnected communication channels, including dedicated Facebook pages, online peer influencers, gay dating apps, an HIV service booking app (I Reserve), and artificial intelligence/chatbots. Two prominent Facebook channels, Xóm Cầu Vồng (Rainbow Village) with 226,000 followers (primarily MSM) and Cô Nàng Gợi Cảm (Be Me. Be Sexy.) with 22,000 followers (targeting transgender women), provide open spaces for these communities to connect, seek support, and learn about health and well-being. Between October 2018 and February 2019, a chatbot was introduced to support OPIs by providing automated responses to queries about PrEP, offering 24-hour assistance. By February 2019, the chatbot had delivered 1,612 instant responses, saving OPIs over 15 hours per month and allowing them to focus on more complex client needs. An online survey of 3,989 users of Xóm Cầu Vồng revealed that 75% had never interacted with a peer or outreach worker, 38% self-assessed as being at substantial risk of HIV, and 35% were motivated to test for HIV due to online content. Among 644 PrEP clients enrolled at Glink Clinic in Ho Chi Minh City between March 2017 and January 2019, 3% reported that online content and interactions motivated them to seek PrEP. These findings underscore the effectiveness of online-to-offline (O2O) strategies in reaching previously unreached populations, building trust, and successfully linking individuals to HIV testing, ART, and PrEP services. In the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the LINKAGES project, funded by USAID and PEPFAR and led by FHI 360, adapted index testing for MSM and female sex workers (FSWs) using two approaches: voluntary partner referral (VPR) and risk network referral (RNR). VPR aligns with WHO guidelines, offering people living with HIV (PLHIV) the opportunity to identify spouses, partners, and children at risk of HIV and refer them for testing and services. RNR extends beyond VPR by allowing PLHIV to informally refer broader social and risk network members for testing without naming or knowing their identities. Between October and December 2018, 191 index cases (66 MSM, 110 FSWs, and 15 clients of FSWs) were offered index testing, and 143 agreed to provide contacts. A total of 169 contacts were listed, and 99 were tested, with high positivity rates observed among clients of FSWs and biological children. Index testing proved effective in improving case detection among key populations in the DRC. In India, the LINKAGES project partnered with the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) to implement index testing for key populations, including MSM, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and FSWs. Two approaches, VPR and RNR, were adapted to engage both individuals enrolled in the targeted intervention (TI) program and those not reached by it. VPR provided PLHIV with options for partner notification and testing while ensuring safety and confidentiality. RNR allowed PLHIV to extend linkages to broader social networks through online and coupon-based referrals. Index testing was implemented in six high HIV-burden districts in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra, with peer navigators facilitating the process in TI sites and community mobilizers in non-TI sites. Challenges related to partner identification and notification were addressed through counseling and violence redressal committees. The case detection rate among spouses was 41%, higher than among other partners, and index testing contributed to 21% of total case detection during a 12-month period. In Jamaica, the LINKAGES project introduced online programs, Talk About Your Business Safely (TABS) and iFlex, to scale up HIV services for MSM and transgender women. These programs, supported by USAID and PEPFAR, are run by local civil society organizations and employ online outreach workers to engage clients through social media platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. Between January and December 2018, over 1,400 individuals were engaged in online conversations, with 452 MSM presenting at physical sites for services. Nearly half of these individuals received HIV testing, with a majority being under 24 years old. Online outreach successfully linked high-risk individuals to testing and care services, demonstrating the potential of digital strategies to reach previously unreached populations. In Malawi, the LINKAGES project implemented VPR and RNR strategies to increase HIV case detection among key populations, including MSM, FSWs, and transgender individuals. These approaches were integrated into community-based testing methods, such as mobile outreach and drop-in centers. Unique identifier codes were used to link sexual partners and biological children to care and treatment services. Between January and February 2019, VPR and RNR achieved higher case detection rates among key populations compared to traditional outreach methods, highlighting their effectiveness in promoting peer-to-peer sharing of information and linking individuals to HIV services. In Kenya, the Eastern Deanery AIDS Relief Program (EDARP), a Catholic faith-based organization, provides integrated HIV and TB prevention, care, and treatment services. EDARP employs a community-to-facility care model, utilizing 1,200 community health workers supervised by 410 clinical staff. Partner notification services (PNS) were re-emphasized in 2019, achieving 100% linkage of HIV-positive clients to care. EDARP also integrated HIV self-testing into its interventions, distributing over 2,000 self-test kits. From July 2018 to June 2019, 119,604 individuals received facility-based HIV testing, with 1,651 adults and 52 children testing positive.
